articles.authors: Luke John Ney; Megan Fry; Trevor Steward; Khalisa Amir Hamzah
articles.abstract: Contemporary models of mental disorders increasingly conceptualise psychopathology as dynamic networks of interacting symptoms, yet these approaches often struggle to account for individual variability in vulnerability and resilience. Recent work has highlighted the role of schemas – enduring cognitive-affective structures – as moderators that shape symptom activation and interactions, suggesting that symptom networks are embedded within deeper structures of the self. Building on schema theory and the Pattern Theory of the Self, which conceptualizes the self as an emergent pattern of interacting life elements, this article proposes a Field Theory of the Self to address the apparent singularity of subjective self-experience and its pervasive effect throughout one’s life. Analogous to physical fields, the current article conceives of the self as a distributed, emergent phenomenon that simultaneously arises from, and constrains, the interactions of its constituent elements. This singular self exerts downward causation across the psychological network, producing recurrent, constrained patterns of schemas, narratives, and symptom dynamics. The Field Theory of the Self aims to provide mechanistic explanations for the persistence and global impact of mental disorders, the idiographic uniqueness of individual experiences, and the nomothetic regularities observed across syndromic categories. By integrating insights from network theory, schema theory, narrative identity, and complex systems, the Field Theory of the Self offers a unifying framework for understanding resilience, vulnerability, and treatment responsiveness, emphasizing the necessity of engaging the self-field as a whole to produce lasting psychological change.

articles.title: Lack of fear acquisition to film clip unconditional stimuli despite contingency awareness: Implications for electrodermal fear conditioning
articles.authors: Mikaela Richardson; Rahul Ashwin Masurkar; Lilyan Tyson; Adam Vasarhelyi; Kalia White; Khalisa Amir Hamzah; Gia Nhi Lam; Sarah Olsson; Ottmar V. Lipp; Casey Agassiz
articles.abstract: Fear conditioning is most commonly assessed by measuring electrodermal activity to a conditioned stimulus (CS) in anticipation of an electric shock or another unconditioned stimulus (US). Replacing the electric shock with aversive film clips is a recent innovation that potentially has higher ecological validity for posttraumatic stress disorder. The present report examined boundary conditions of this new paradigm across two experiments, with a particular focus on the effectiveness of film clip versus electric shock USs in promoting physiological fear conditioning. In Experiment 1, we tested whether fear acquisition was influenced by the inclusion of a shock US, prior exposure to a longer trauma film, or the use of face versus shape conditioned stimuli (CSs). Fear acquisition was enhanced by the inclusion of a shock US and to a lesser extent by prior trauma film exposure; however, conditioning in groups using film clip USs alone was characterised by lack of conditioned electrodermal responding. Experiment 2 investigated whether this absence of conditioned responding reflected reduced contingency awareness by measuring online US expectancy across film-based and shock-based US conditions. Despite equivalent US expectancy, CS pleasantness, and subjective US ratings across groups, conditioned electrodermal responses during acquisition were observed only in the shock US condition. Differences between groups may be explained by differences in salivary cortisol reactivity, with higher cortisol responses following acquisition in the shock group. Together, these findings indicate that shock USs increase physiological arousal, which appears to be essential for electrodermal reactivity, irrespective of conditioned learning processes. This finding has potentially important implications for the interpretation of electrodermal measurement in fear conditioning paradigms.

articles.title: DBT Skills Video Intervention for Chinese/Chinese American College Students: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.authors: Qingqing Yin; Shireen L. Rizvi
articles.abstract: Psychotherapy delivered in its traditional format is unlikely to benefit Asian Americans (AA) due to low rates of treatment utilization and retention. Brief videos teaching Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) skills provides an alternative avenue to disseminate emotion regulation resources. The integration of behavioral change strategies and Zen Buddhist philosophies (e.g., acceptance) in DBT may also be culturally appealing to some AA subgroups. In this study, we evaluated the acceptability/usability and outcomes of a video-based DBT skills intervention among a sample of Chinese/Chinese American individuals. The intervention was comprised of 14 brief animated videos of DBT skills. A total of 91 Chinese/Chinese American college students, not currently receiving treatment, completed daily assessment for four weeks and were randomized to receive (1) assessment-only (n = 29), (2) acceptance-oriented followed by change-oriented skills videos (n = 32), or (3) change-oriented followed by acceptance-oriented skills videos (n = 30). Self-reports and engagement behaviors supported the acceptability/usability of the intervention, which was not found to differ between change- or acceptance-oriented skills videos. Compared to the control group, the intervention groups showed more favorable outcomes related to the distress and management of emotional experiences. This study provides insights of acceptable and effective ways to address mental health needs of Asian/Asian Americans while extending the scarce literature on this topic.

articles.title: Comments on Réale, Dall, and Dingemanse (2026). Praise, and a pathway for integrating the study of personality evolution
articles.authors: Alexander Weiss
articles.abstract: Réale, Dall, and Dingemanse have contributed a valuable commentary, both in terms of clarifying how to (and not to) consider “personality traits” and in, perhaps unknowingly, providing a glimmer of a bridge that can unify the study of animal and human personality. My comments reveal the bridge in all its glory.

articles.title: A SOCIAL IDENTITY MODEL OF LEADERSHIP DEVELOPMENT IMPLEMENTATION
articles.authors: Blake McMillan; S. Alexander Haslam; Tyree Mitchell; Niklas K Steffens; Kim Olivia Peters
articles.abstract:
Despite substantial investment in leadership development, organizations often struggle to
implement relevant programs effectively. This reflects the fact that the success of program
implementation is contingent on identity dynamics. Building on the Social Identity Model of
Leadership, the ASPIRe model, and evidence-based programs such as 5R that apply these
principles, we argue that, to be effective, implementation needs to ensure that the approach
makes sense for “us”, aligns with who “we” are, and fits with “our” leadership. To guide this
process, we present a Social Identity Model of Leadership Development Implementation
(SIMoLDI) which specifies four phases of effective implementation: (1) identity activation, (2)
identity alignment, (3) identity actualization, and (4) identity anchoring. Each phase draws on
distinct identity leadership components: prototypicality, entrepreneurship, advancement, and
impresarioship. The principles we outline have general relevance in providing a practical, theory-
informed framework for translating leadership development initiatives into sustainable practice,
while being particularly applicable when leadership development is focused on building
collective capability.

articles.title: Prototype principle explains aesthetics for general visual experiences beyond isolated objects
articles.authors: Yi-Chia Chen; Shuhao Fu; Derek Feng; Moriah Taylor; Jeff Chang; Xiaoyang Chi; Hongjing Lu
articles.abstract: A salient aspect of our daily visual experiences is the aesthetic impressions. Why do we enjoy some views but not others? Researchers have found visual attributes that we enjoy seeing for colors, shapes, and objects, and even for human faces and bodies; however, aesthetic preferences for holistic visual experiences—views that encompass many different objects and attributes—remain largely undescribed. What principles govern holistic visual aesthetics beyond preferences for certain objects or features? We found computational evidence in support of the prototype principle for visual aesthetics. We measure each view’s prototypicality based on its average similarity to a large reference set of images in feature spaces from pretrained deep convolutional neural networks (AlexNet and VGG-16). For views consisting of inanimate content, the more prototypical the high-level visual representations are, the more aesthetically pleasing the views appear. This prototype effect suggests a functional answer to why we like what we like: We like typical visual experiences that are common, safe, or neutral. Thus, aesthetic preferences from holistic visual experiences are systematic, explainable, and reflect the underlying organization of visual representations of the world. Our method demonstrates a new way to explore both vision and aesthetics using computational models—besides investigating specific visual properties or isolated objects, we can also explore the organization of visual representations and aesthetic experiences holistically, getting us one step closer to understanding how we see, what we like, and why we like what we like in everyday life.

articles.title: Geographically Segregated Culture is associated with Lower Mobility, Weaker Democracy, and Risk of Civil Conflict
articles.authors: Cindel J. M. White; Michael Muthukrishna
articles.abstract: Stable nations require strangers to coordinate and cooperate despite cultural differences. Using the Cultural Fixation Index (CFST) on World Values Survey data (more than 260,000 participants; 95 countries; 2005–2022), we quantified within-country cultural distances between regions, ethnicities, religious groups, education levels, and social classes, to predict various measures of social mobility, democracy, and civil conflict. A pre-registered multiverse analysis (54,600 model specifications; 100 model families; 6 demographic groupings; 6 outcome measures) showed only one robust pattern of negative societal outcomes: larger cultural distance between geographic regions is associated with higher corruption, weaker democracy, lower social mobility, and greater risk of civil conflict. Distances between ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic groups were mostly benign, and educational distance was often associated with better outcomes. The results imply that what matters is not diversity per se, but whether culturally distinct groups are geographically segregated and therefore less likely to regularly interact to negotiate the cultural traits needed for cooperation and coordination.

articles.title: Relationship between sensory processing sensitivity and rejection sensitivity and their association with mental health
articles.authors: Jacob I. Stephens; Lindsey B. Hinkle; Zoe A. Childers-Rockey; Charlie Rioux
articles.abstract: Sensory processing sensitivity (SPS) and rejection sensitivity (RS) are two distinct sensitivity-related traits that have each been associated with poorer mental health. However, little research has examined how these constructs relate to one another or whether they uniquely contribute to mental health. This study examined the association between SPS and RS and their independent relationships with mental distress and well-being in an online sample of 565 adults. Participants self-reported SPS, RS, psychological distress, and well-being. Correlations and multiple linear regressions were conducted to examine associations between SPS, RS, distress, and well-being, both before and after adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. While both traits independently predicted psychological distress, RS demonstrated a stronger and more robust association with psychological well-being after accounting for sociodemographic factors. These findings suggest that assessing both SPS and RS may improve understanding of individual differences in mental health and inform more targeted prevention and intervention strategies.

articles.title: A rapid assessment of pragmatic abilities and cognitive substrates: The German APACS Brief
articles.authors: Lena Sophie Wilkens; Laura Anna Ciaccio; Thomas Picht; Marta Bosia; Giorgio Arcara; Valentina Bambini; Rosario Tomasello
articles.abstract:
Background
Clinical evaluation of language abilities is central to diagnosing impairments in neurological and neuropsychiatric conditions, such as brain injuries, Parkinson’s disease, or schizophrenia. However, assessment tools predominantly target formal structural aspects of language, including phonological, lexical-semantic, and syntactic processing, while pragmatic and communicative abilities remain underrepresented, despite consistent evidence of their vulnerability across clinical populations. This gap is largely due to the scarcity of standardized and rapid tools for pragmatic assessment and the inherent difficulty of measuring context-dependent communicative abilities.
Aim
This study aimed to develop and validate the German adaptation of the Assessment of Pragmatic Abilities and Cognitive Substrates Brief (APACS Brief-De), a 10-minute screening tool originally created in Italian, assessing discourse production and comprehension of figurative language (metaphor and humor) in German-speaking contexts, to evaluate the psychometric properties, usability, and cross-linguistic applicability of the instrument.
Methods
Adopting a culturally sensitive translation approach, a standard and a multiple-choice APACS Brief-De were developed, each with an alternate form to allow for repeated assessments, which were administered remotely to healthy German-speaking adults.
Results
The APACS Brief-De Multiple Choice showed good consistency, reliability, validity, and equivalence between forms. Increasing age and lower global cognitive functioning were significantly associated with reduced pragmatic performance.  The comparisons with the Italian standard form confirmed statistical equivalence, underscoring the robustness of the tool across languages. Age- and education-adjusted normative cut-off scores are provided for clinical interpretation.
Conclusions
APACS Brief-De offers a rapid and valid tool for assessing global pragmatic abilities, well suited for integration into routine clinical practice, and represents a significant step toward crosslinguistic standardization of pragmatic assessment.

articles.title: Reduced speech-to-song transformation for native-language speech in Mandarin Chinese listeners
articles.authors: Makiko Sadakata; Yuzhu Gu
articles.abstract: Why does a listener's linguistic background shape whether repeated speech comes to sound like music? Previous studies have reported that speakers of tonal languages experience a weaker Speech-to-Song (STS) transformation, in which repeated speech comes to sound increasingly musical. It remains unclear, however, whether this reduction reflects a general property of tonal-language listeners or arises specifically when they hear their native language. We compared native Mandarin Chinese, English, and Dutch listeners' responses to English speech, Mandarin Chinese speech, and non-speech stimuli (data collected 2024– 2026) before and after repeated presentation. All groups reliably experienced the STS transformation. Critically, however, the transformation was markedly reduced only when native Mandarin Chinese listeners heard Mandarin Chinese speech. The same listeners showed a typical transformation for English speech, and English and Dutch listeners showed comparable transformations for both languages. Furthermore, this reduction disappeared when linguistic information was removed while preserving the original pitch contours. These findings indicate that reduced transformation is not a general characteristic of tonal-language listeners but depends on whether pitch remains available for lexical interpretation. The results suggest that the linguistic function of pitch constrains its reinterpretation as melody, a pattern consistent with predictive-coding accounts of speech and music perception.

articles.title: The Mind's Eye of the Adopter: Visual Stereotypes of Dogs and Cats
articles.authors: Lindsay Palmer; Daniel N Albohn; Alexander Todorov; Anamarie C. Johnson; Reginald B. Adams; Joseph C. Brandenburg; Clive DL Wynne
articles.abstract: The influence of visual appearance on pet adoption is poorly understood, partially due to inconsistent findings. We examined visual biases in the appearance of dogs and cats using a novel data-driven method that leverages generative AI to visualize mental prototypes at both the individual and group levels. The results demonstrated both strong idiosyncratic preferences and shared, group-level consistencies, offering an explanation for previously reported inconsistencies. Importantly, we found that greater similarity between images of real shelter animals and the group prototypes of “adoptable” dogs and cats, as well as “friendly” dogs, was associated with a shorter time in the shelter before adoption. This study provides novel evidence for the interplay between idiosyncratic variation and shared biases in shaping visual stereotypes of companion animals.

articles.title: Beyond the Label: Capturing Nuanced Head Nod Distinctions in ASL and TİD via Pose Estimation and DTW
articles.authors: Serpil Karabüklü; Emre Hakguder; Diane Brentari
articles.abstract: Sign language research has long recognized that head nods participate in a wide range of linguistic functions, including prosody, semantics, and discourse. However, these movements are typically described using categorical labels (e.g., head nod), obscuring how continuous movement maps onto linguistic function and making it difficult to determine whether different functions recruit the same articulatory gesture or distinct kinematic realizations. This study investigates whether head nods associated with different linguistic functions differ in their internal movement organization and whether these distinctions are shared across sign languages. We analyzed 608 head nods produced by 19 Deaf signers of American Sign Language (ASL) and Turkish Sign Language (TİD). Head movement trajectories were extracted using computer vision-based keypoint estimation and examined through complementary analyses of kinematic features and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). Results revealed three main findings. First, semantic and prosodic head nods systematically differed in their kinematic organization: semantic head nods exhibited greater peak prominence, whereas prosodic head nods exhibited greater trough prominence in both languages. Second, these form-function mappings were shared across ASL and TİD, suggesting common principles linking kinematic structure to linguistic function. Third, trajectory-based analyses revealed language-specific differences that were not captured by individual kinematic features: prosodic head nods showed distinct trajectories across languages, whereas semantic head nods remained highly similar. These findings demonstrate that linguistic distinctions are encoded not only in individual movement features but also in the temporal organization of continuous movement. More broadly, the findings suggest that linguistic information in sign languages is organized not only across articulatory channels but also within the temporal organization of movement. Rather than the gesture label itself, specific kinematic realizations constitute the relevant units linking continuous movement to linguistic function.

articles.title: Assessing Fairness in AI-Assisted Writing Scoring: Two Indices for Quantifying the Magnitude of Group Differences
articles.authors: Guanyu Chen; Sirui Wu; Chiyu Zhang; Amery D. Wu
articles.abstract: Fairness evaluation in automated essay scoring (AES) requires more than determining whether group differences exist. It also requires evidence about how large those differences are, which group they favor, and whether they warrant further attention. This study introduces two model-level indices, Conditional Mean Disparity (CMD) and Conditional Odds Disparity (COD), for evaluating group differences in predicted writing scores after accounting for human-rated proficiency. CMD quantifies disparity on the predicted score scale, whereas COD quantifies disparity using the relative odds of receiving higher predicted scores. The indices were demonstrated using writing samples from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus and four AES systems representing traditional statistical modeling, deep learning, and prompt-based large language model scoring. The findings showed that CMD and COD provided interpretable estimates of disparity magnitude across systems and captured information that was not reflected in scoring performance alone. By emphasizing the size and direction of observed group differences, the proposed indices can support fairness evaluation, model comparison, and decisions about whether further examination is needed.

articles.title: A Behavioural Investigation of Multisensory Integration in Youth with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
articles.authors: Carolynn Hare; Bernice Leung; Glenda Zhai; YuHe Li; Ryan A Stevenson
articles.abstract: Multisensory integration is a key sensory process which has a role in cognitive development. Multisensory integration has been demonstrated to be affected in ADHD largely in adults, but findings have been inconsistent. In this study, we examined whether multisensory integration differed in youth (ages 4-17) with ADHD (n=53) and without ADHD (n=60) using three different behavioural tasks (i.e., SIFI, McGurk, and speech-in-noise). No group differences were found in the SIFI, but ADHD youth showed reduced susceptibility to the McGurk illusion compared to neurotypical (NT) youth. The speech-in-noise task revealed no differences in multisensory gain, though hyperactive-impulsive traits were trending negatively related to phoneme accuracy. Overall, the results suggest reduced multisensory integration in youth with ADHD, using tasks involving speech stimuli. These results suggest that stimulus complexity may be important to examine for multisensory integration in ADHD, and further, multisensory integration may be affected across development in ADHD.

articles.title: Child Multilingualisms Beyond WEIRD Contexts: Evidence from Asia and Africa
articles.authors: Alexandra Paquette; Leher Singh
articles.abstract: Who is the language learner represented in language acquisition research? Despite the prevalence and diversity of multilingual childhoods, theories of early language development remain grounded in monolinguals from Euro-American contexts, while multilingual research has concentrated on limited populations/settings. This review examines multilingual language development during the first three years across Asia and Africa, attending to diversity within and between regions. Research on input, speech perception, word recognition, and vocabulary indicate that multilingual infants flexibly adapt to linguistic ecologies, but vary in developmental pathways. We argue that multilingualism should be conceptualized not as a categorical characteristic, but as a multidimensional ecology structured by language combinations, caregiving arrangements, social functions, socioeconomic conditions, and colonial histories. We conclude with a research agenda that broadens empirical and linguistic coverage, improves measurement of multilingual experiences, and centers community-informed priorities. A globally adequate science of language development requires building theory from children’s diverse multilingual realities.

articles.title: For Whom Do School-Based Mindfulness Programs Work? The Role of Personality in Adolescent Intervention Outcomes
articles.authors: Maria Anna Wasylkowska; Dorota Kobylinska; Julian Mituniewicz; Szymon Szumiał; Pawel Holas
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objectives
School-based mindfulness programs (SBMPs) are increasingly implemented to support adolescent mental health, yet evidence for their effectiveness remains mixed. Recent research suggests that average effects may obscure meaningful variability in outcomes across individuals. The present study aimed to examine both the overall effectiveness of a 6-week SBMP and the role of personality traits in predicting individual differences in intervention outcomes. 
Method
This quasi-experimental study included 122 adolescents aged 12–14 years from 14 school classes, assigned to either an intervention group or a wait-list control group. Outcomes were assessed at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and 3-month follow-up, including anxiety, emotion regulation difficulties, well-being, mindfulness, psychological distress, and self-compassion. Personality traits (neuroticism, extraversion, and openness) were examined as predictors of differential response to the intervention using latent class growth analysis and logistic regression. 
Results 
At the group level, the SBMP did not produce significant effects across the examined outcomes compared to the control condition. However, person-centered analyses revealed meaningful heterogeneity in response patterns. Adolescents characterized by higher neuroticism and lower extraversion were more likely to show improvements across multiple domains, including reduced anxiety and psychological distress and increased well-being and mindfulness. Additionally, lower openness predicted improvement in psychological distress. These findings suggest that intervention effects were not uniform but concentrated among adolescents with greater baseline vulnerability.
Conclusions 
These results indicate that the effectiveness of SBMPs may depend less on average effects and more on individual differences in responsiveness. Mindfulness training may be particularly beneficial for adolescents with specific personality profiles associated with higher psychological vulnerability. These results highlight the importance of moving beyond universal approaches toward more targeted implementation of mindfulness-based programs in school settings. 
Keywords: mindfulness, adolescence, personality, training, SBMPs

articles.title: Ordinality and dyscalculia: what do we actually know?
articles.authors: Declan Devlin; Natalia Dubinkina; Pirjo Aunio
articles.abstract: Over the past two decades, there has been increasing interest in the role of order processing in developmental dyscalculia. In this review, we consider the literature on how people with dyscalculia process ordinal information and the cognitive and affective factors that contribute to observed deficits. Across studies, children and adults with dyscalculia consistently show impaired performance on a range of order processing tasks, including symbolic numerical order verification, order production, and event ordering tasks. These findings have led some researchers to conclude that dyscalculia is characterised by a general deficit in order processing. However, other evidence suggests these deficits may emerge only for certain sequences, implying more specific underlying mechanisms (e.g., working memory deficits). We argue that these contrasting conclusions largely reflect the relatively coarse level at which order processing has typically been investigated and thus encourage more fine-grained approaches that distinguish between tasks, items, and their underlying cognitive demands.

articles.title: Two Identities, One Alliance? Catalysts and Constraints of Dual Identification for Allyship Formation
articles.authors: Jonas R. Kunst; John Dovidio
articles.abstract: Allyship—actions by advantaged-group members supporting marginalized groups—is shaped by how groups define “us.” Common-ingroup appeals (e.g., “we are all Americans”) broaden goodwill but often obscure power imbalances, stalling action. Dual-identity appeals (e.g., “Black and American”) can mobilize allies by highlighting injustice. Yet, they risk triggering suspicions of divided loyalty when groups feel threatened. Integrating social, cultural, and evolutionary psychology, we map the catalysts that facilitate and the constraints that inhibit dual-identity allyship. This framework emphasizes reciprocal influences between groups and highlights the importance of marginalized-group receptivity to allyship efforts. We translate these processes into an actionable policy matrix based on perceived injustice and intergroup threat. The matrix specifies when to emphasize dual identities for justice, when to prioritize threat reduction to ensure receptivity, or when to sequence both approaches. Clarifying when a dual identity sustains allyship equips practitioners with tools for lasting intergroup cooperation.

articles.title: Ten simple rules for achieving computational reproducibility in cognitive neuroscience
articles.authors: Gaurav Mahajan; Caroline J Charpentier; Valentin Guigon
articles.abstract:
Computational research depends on complex, linked operations. In cognitive neuroscience, these operations often combine multiple data types, specialized toolboxes, custom scripts, and changing computing environments. Open science practices, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) principles, and data standardization have improved how research objects are shared and described. However, they do not guarantee that the same analysis can be rerun to reconstruct the original result. This limitation becomes more consequential as AI-assisted coding tools are accelerating code development, with the potential to strengthen good practices, but also to amplify weak ones. Related problems have long been addressed in software engineering and machine learning operations through practices that make code, data, environments, and execution steps traceable. Drawing from these practices, we present ten simple rules for achieving computational reproducibility in cognitive neuroscience. We emphasize simple, low-cost decisions that can be implemented early and scaled as
projects become more complex.

articles.title: When Does Cognitive Ability Matter for Vote Choice? Ideological Orientation as a Moderator in the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Till Lubczyk; André Kretzschmar
articles.abstract: Cognitive ability predicts vote choice, but does it do so equally across the ideological spectrum? In a preregistered longitudinal study, U.S. young adults (N = 594) completed a broad cognitive ability assessment and five ideology measures (right-wing authoritarianism, social dominance orientation, social and economic conservatism, political self-placement) before the 2024 presidential election and reported their vote afterwards. Lower cognitive ability and stronger right-wing orientations each predicted voting for Trump, replicating prior findings; these associations held when controlling for demographics, including education and household income. Critically, Local Structural Equation Modeling revealed that ideology moderated the cognitive ability-vote choice association: it was robust among liberal and moderate voters but faded to near zero at high levels of right-wing commitment for four of five measures. The findings are consistent with motivated cognition accounts and challenge the assumption that reasoning ability plays a uniform role in electoral decision-making.

articles.title: A dynamic theory of multi-agent goal pursuit in continuous time and space
articles.authors: Anderson K. Fitch; Peter D. Kvam
articles.abstract: Many of the goals that people pursue in everyday life involve dynamic social interactions with others who have their own latent goals. Modeling how these goals manifest in behavior and how different goals interact with one another is central to effectively explaining and predicting the dynamics of human interactions. In this paper, we develop a theory that postulates a balance of global and local objectives driving behavior, combining elements of control theory and approach-avoidance to predict complex movement and dyadic interactions in real time. We apply this model to explain movement in a continuous control task, where participants use a joystick to accomplish a variety of direct (attack / avoid / inspect the other player) and indirect (defend a location from the other player / herd the other player to a location) goals. In the first experiment, participants interacted with a computer opponent. In the second experiment, participants interacted with other participants who had an independent goal. The goal pursuit model successfully accounted for player movement across time as people dynamically adapted to their opponent's behavior, providing insights into participants' trial-specific and person-specific priorities. In addition, the model parameters were used to identify participants' latent goals in both the single-player and two-player tasks, yielding superior performance to classifiers based on raw behavior. Put together, the model can support real-time behavioral prediction and intent inference even in complex multi-agent interactions faced by humans and social AI.

articles.title: Hive Immunity: How the Social Brain Aligns Immune Systems for Collective Protection
articles.authors: Simone Shamay-Tsoory
articles.abstract: Pathogens create a fundamental tension in social life. Although close social bonds enable caregiving and group cohesion, they also increase exposure to infection. To address this tension, extant theories have suggested that sickness behaviors evolved primarily to counteract infection through avoidance and withdrawal as protective responses to illness. However, emerging evidence suggests that illness can also elicit approach toward caregivers. Here, I propose the immune alignment theory, which suggests that immune responses may become coordinated between infected individuals and their close social partners. The theory holds that perceiving sickness in close others, may trigger matched preparatory immune changes in the uninfected observer. This response may facilitate caregiving while enhancing self-protection. In terms of neural correlates, immune alignment is likely mediated by brain–immune and brain-to-brain interactions and supported by neural systems involved in reward, salience, and interbrain synchrony. The immune alignment theory offers a framework for understanding how social relationships shape immune regulation beyond the individual body, with implications for caregiving, psychopathology, and collective health. Direct empirical tests of immune alignment remain an important direction for future research.

articles.title: Visual information selected during active viewing is sufficient to drive similar aesthetic evaluations in passive viewers: Evidence from ‘attentional transplants’
articles.authors: Hong B Nguyen; Benjamin van Buren
articles.abstract: Aesthetically evaluating a scene typically involves active viewing, where one controls what one sees and when. Active viewing includes planning where to look, moving, and selecting information—any of which could influence aesthetic judgments. Using a method of ‘attentional transplants’, we show that information selected during active viewing is sufficient to cause similar aesthetic evaluations even in passive viewers: First, online ‘donors’ actively viewed scenes through a cursor-controlled window and rated their aesthetic pleasingness. Next, new ‘recipients’ passively viewed the scenes through windows replaying the viewing pattern of the donor who liked the scene most, or least. Recipients gave substantially higher ratings to scenes after seeing the selection patterns of donors who most liked (vs. disliked) them. Subsequent experiments found that selection patterns which drive greater liking allow better prediction of upcoming information. Thus, visual information selected during active viewing, independent of active control, is sufficient to drive aesthetic evaluations.

articles.title: Feeling the way to words: Parents' speech and touch cues highlight word-to-world mappings of body parts. Language Learning and Development,
articles.authors: Ruth Tincoff; Amanda Seidl; Lauren Buckley; Christa Wojcik; Alejandrina Cristia; Alicia Horton-Mastin
articles.abstract:
Touch cues might facilitate infants’ early word comprehension and explain why body part words
emerge so early. Parents were instructed to teach their infants, 4- to 5-month-olds or 10- to 11-
month-olds, nonce words for body parts and a contrast object but were given no instructions
about the use of touch. Parents spontaneously touched target body parts in close timing to
uttering the target nonce words. They did not show this alignment for unrelated touches and
nonce words. Moreover, when parents used this temporally synchronized speech and touch input,
infants looked more frequently to the target locations on their bodies and to their parent’s faces
compared to when the input was mismatched or only speech. Similar to other research on parents' use of speech and gesture input, these results show how parents use multimodal speech-touch input and raise the possibility that infants use touch cues to segment and map early words.

articles.title: Developmental Changes in Infants’ Ability to Cope with Dialect Variation in Word Segmentation
articles.authors: Rachel Schmale; Alejandrina Cristia; Amanda Seidl; Elizabeth Johnson; Alicia Horton-Mastin
articles.abstract: Towards the end of their first year of life, infants learn to ignore variation in sounds not present, or not functional, in their ambient language. Specifically, overly specified word representations are thought to give way to others with which learners can cope better with indexical variation, such as voice and affect, which are not relevant to word identity. This developmental change may help infants in their second year to more efficiently process the ambient language and thus make rapid gains in vocabulary. One particular kind of variability that infants must accommodate is that of dialectal accent, since most children will encounter speakers from different regions and backgrounds. In this study, we explore developmental changes in infants’ ability to recognize words in continuous speech by familiarizing them with words spoken by a speaker of their own region (North Midland American English) or a different region (Southern Ontario Canadian English), and testing them with passages spoken by a speaker of the opposite dialectal accent. Our results demonstrate that 12- but not 9-month-olds readily recognize words in the face of dialectal variation.

articles.title: A Large-Scale Analysis of Temporal Patterns in Children’s Purported Past-Life Memories: Shorter Intervals Following Unexpected Deaths
articles.authors: Saeedeh Sadeghi; Marieta Pehlivanova; Philip J. Cozzolino
articles.abstract: Cases of the Reincarnation Type (CORT) involve individuals—typically young children—who report memories they claim are from previous lives. One recurring observation is the apparent “intermission time” between the death of the putatively identified previous person and the child’s birth. However, systematic large-scale analyses of related factors remain limited. The present study analyzed 1,678 cases with an ostensibly identified past person, to test whether intermission time correlates with death characteristics and whether any observed association persists after accounting for variables likely to facilitate bias. Death unexpectedness and naturalness were both significantly associated with intermission time (both p < .001), with median intervals decreasing from approximately 21 months at the lowest level of death unexpectedness to 12 months at the highest level—representing about a 40–45% reduction. The unexpectedness of death remained the strongest unique predictor in multiple regression. The association persisted across five moderation analyses examining verification quality, memory contamination, family association, social status motivation, and reincarnation belief. Notably, the effect was stronger among families without reincarnation beliefs, opposite to what a cultural construction hypothesis would predict. Although the data are observational and subject to potential selection biases, our findings replicate and extend prior reports, suggesting that temporal patterns in CORT cases may reflect a systematic phenomenon not readily accounted for by existing psychosocial frameworks. Further research using contemporary cases is needed to clarify underlying mechanisms and theoretical implications.

articles.title: Training adolescents on climate action fosters behavioral change across social concerns and generations
articles.authors: Esther Blanco; Adria Bronchal; Aida Guerrero Tort; Natalie Struwe
articles.abstract:
Climate action has a strong cooperative component: many mitigation choices carry no private payoff, yet collectively generate broad social benefits. Here, we propose a new paradigm for behavioral and educational climate interventions that targets the cooperative decision-making competencies underlying climate action, and test it in a field intervention among high-school students (n=762) and their parents (n=416), using a multi-method assessment of cooperation and climate-action outcomes. The intervention had a direct positive effect on adolescents’ donations to pro-environmental causes, measured with real monetary stakes, and increased hope and mitigation behavior among students in green-network schools. It also generated positive spillovers beyond climate: donations to poverty and health concerns rose across the full sample, and strategic peer cooperation increased among girls. One year later, spillovers on other social concerns and on hope in addressing the climate
crisis persisted. The impacts of the intervention further multiplied within households: parents of treated adolescents gained climate knowledge, and parents whose children attended green-network schools increased their own pro-environmental donations and mitigation behavior. Training cooperation for climate action can thus offer a durable pathway to greener, fairer lifestyles, with adolescents acting as agents of change within their communities.

articles.title: Why Conventional Practices in Construct Validation Provide Limited Evidence of Construct Validity
articles.authors: Leon Patrick Wendt; Steffen Müller
articles.abstract: The construct validity of psychometric instruments is a foundation of psychological science, as instruments should measure the intended theoretical constructs rather than unintended ones. Yet it has been argued that conventional construct validation practices often produce weak, uninformative evidence and fall short of the strong, risk-bearing tests emphasized by validity theorists. Extant evidence often cannot support meaningful claims about construct validity. We introduce the EVE-CV framework, based on Meehl's logic of hypothesis testing, for evaluating the evidential value (or quality) of construct validation efforts. Evidential value refers to the extent to which conducting a test of construct validity is expected to shift confidence among the proposed construct interpretation and plausible alternative interpretations. The framework translates three logical requirements for evidential value into six practical criteria for designing and evaluating construct validation studies. We also use the framework to explain how three conventional validation practices contribute to low evidential value: using conceptual placeholders, overrelying on generic psychometric methods, and revising the nomological network based entirely on evidence generated by the measure under validation. We argue that these practices are commonly used to portray instruments as “validated”, while providing only nominal evidence of construct validity.

articles.title: Gradual delays do not affect the tolerability of a smartphone friction intervention
articles.authors: Sabrina Fay Norwood; David Joachim Grüning; Frederik Riedel; Malte Elson
articles.abstract: Friction-based digital interventions reduce unwanted smartphone behaviour by interrupting automatic app-opening sequences, but substantial attrition rates limit their real-world impact. One proposed strategy for improving retention is to gradually increase intervention intensity, allowing users to adapt before encountering the full intervention dose. We tested this in a preregistered six-week field experiment (N = 1,641) in which new users of the smartphone friction app one sec were randomly assigned to one of four delay escalation schedules ranging from immediate full-dose exposure (10 seconds throughout) to gradual escalation (3 → 6 → 10 seconds). Retention was low and relatively similar across conditions (65–70% dropout), with no significant difference between any of three escalation schedules and the standard full-dose condition. Exploratory analyses likewise found no association between delay duration and weekly dropout. However, among participants who remained engaged, longer delays were associated with higher rates of dismissed app opening attempts, suggesting that delay duration influenced behaviour without improving retention. These findings do not support gradual intensity escalation as a retention strategy and instead suggest that intervention characteristics may optimise different outcomes. While delay duration appears useful for shaping behaviour among retained users, retention itself may depend more on the introduction of interruption than its precise duration.

articles.title: Validation of the VOICE (Visible Opportunities for Infants to Connect and Engage) infant mental health observation tool
articles.authors: Victoria Gray Armstrong; Neil McLaren; Josephine Ross
articles.abstract: This paper offers a robust validation of the VOICE observation tool; a novel, open source, infant mental health evaluation tool, assessing the quality of caregiver-infant interactions through direct observation of the infants agentive and relational experiences. Developed and tested with a broad pool of practitioners and families in the context of an art-therapy based attachment intervention in the UK, the VOICE tool offers a well-fitted three-factor instrument of infant mental health, separating observation of infant’s agency, engagement and development opportunities from their relational opportunities, and offering a global reflection on the infant’s typical experience of the caregiver-infant relationship. Meeting academic and clinical standards for intra and inter-rater reliability and criterion and convergent validity, this clinically sensitive tool captured both identified challenges (discriminating universal dyads from those referred to support) and clinically relevant improvement in attachment relations (capturing change in the infant’s experience). Demonstrating discriminant validity, and highlighting the importance of direct observation of the infant’s reality, the tool assessed infant mental health in a manner distinct from commonly utilised parental report measures. Clinical teams found the tool to be both feasible and valuable, redressing the lack of accessible infant-centred outcome measures, and foregrounding the ‘voice of the infant’ in clinical care.

articles.title: Mechanisms underlying accent accommodation in early word learning: evidence for general expansion
articles.authors: Rachel Schmale; Amanda Seidl; Alejandrina Cristia; Alicia Horton-Mastin
articles.abstract: Previous work reveals that toddlers can accommodate a novel accent after hearing it for only a brief period of time. A common assumption is that children, like adults, cope with nonstandard pronunciations by relying on words they know (e.g. ‘this person pronounces sock as sack, therefore by black she meant block’). In this paper, we assess whether toddlers might additionally use a general expansion strategy, whereby they simply accept non-standard pronunciations when variability is expected. We exposed a group of 24-month-old English-learning toddlers to variability in indexical cues (very diverse voices from native English talkers), and another to variability in social cues (very diverse-looking silent actors); neither group was familiarized with the target novel accent. At test, both groups succeeded in recognizing a novel word when spoken in the novel accent. Thus, even when no lexical cues are available, variability can prepare young children for non-standard pronunciations.

articles.title: The hyperarticulation hypothesis of infant-directed speech
articles.authors: Alicia Horton-Mastin; Alejandrina Cristia; Amanda Seidl
articles.abstract: Typically, the point vowels [i,ɑ,u] are acoustically more peripheral in infant-directed speech (IDS) compared to adult-directed speech (ADS). If caregivers seek to highlight lexically relevant contrasts in IDS, then two sounds that are contrastive should become more distinct, whereas two sounds that are surface realizations of the same underlying sound category should not. To test this prediction, vowels that are phonemically contrastive ([i–ɪ] and [eɪ–ε]), vowels that map onto the same underlying category ([æ–æ̃] and [ε–ε̃]), and the point vowels [i,ɑ,u] were elicited in IDS and ADS by American English mothers of two age groups of infants (four- and eleven-month-olds). As in other work, point vowels were produced in more peripheral positions in IDS compared to ADS. However, there was little evidence of hyperarticulation per se (e.g. [i–ɪ] was hypoarticulated). We suggest that across-the-board lexically based hyperarticulation is not a necessary feature of IDS.

articles.title: Choosing isn’t always a walk in the park: Dog food preference versus choice
articles.authors: Julia Espinosa; Madeline Helmer Pelgrim; Daphna Buchsbaum
articles.abstract: Preferences underpin a range of fitness behaviors for many mammals such as foraging, object interactions, and even social relationships. Despite the ubiquity of domestic dogs in modern culture, the basis for preferences driving their behavior and choices are not well understood. Past work has found that dogs perceive and respond to certain characteristics of items, specifically an object's familiarity and quality when making choices. However, in the real world, these characteristics don't exist in isolation, and understanding the interaction between familiarity and valuation as they relate to object choice can provide insight into how dogs make decisions. We aimed to explore how item familiarity and quality intersect to form dogs’ preferences for one food over another in a series of two-alternative forced choice tasks. Over three studies, dogs (N = 125) were presented with a classic preference test between two items of unequal quality (Study 1), systematic pairings of four items that contrasted familiarity and quality (Study 2), and aggregates of two items of unequal quality (Study 3). Overall, we found that dogs' choices were driven only by the quality of the food item, and the prior familiarity of the item did not impact choice behavior. Determining what motivates dogs and contributes to their preferences has implications for understanding decision-making at large, as well as for advancing canine science.

articles.title: Does self-projection have a dominant temporal direction? In nine countries, people feel more similar to their future than past selves
articles.authors: Jareef Martuza; Simen Bø; Helge Thorbjørnsen; Hallgeir Sjåstad
articles.abstract: Do you project your current self—the person you are today—equally across time? Compared to the present, 12 studies (total N = 11,416) reveal that people feel more similar to their future selves than their equidistant past selves. This future-oriented asymmetry in self-projection is directionally consistent across nine countries, with variation in effect size, and holds across different time horizons. Time-asymmetric self-projection covaries with higher levels of emotional connection between present and future selves and lower levels of perceived future self-change. We also provide preliminary causal-chain evidence for perceived self-change as a process by experimentally manipulating self-change beliefs. The future-oriented asymmetry appears to be self-focused, as it does not extend to others. Finally, future-oriented self-projection can lead to miscalibrated expectations: People expect their future selves to be more satisfied with hypothetical decisions made in the present than they currently would be with the same decisions in the past.

articles.title: Lexicological salience in ideophone semantics: Toward an onomasiological turn
articles.authors: Thomas Van Hoey
articles.abstract: Ideophones have become a principal testing ground for research on linguistic iconicity. Existing work has extensively examined their marked formal properties, depictive functions, and sensory semantics, but has paid comparatively little attention to their lexical organization. This paper argues that ideophones should be studied not only semasiologically, as mappings from form to meaning, but also onomasiologically, as lexical resources from which speakers select expressions for conceptualizing sensory experience. Building on Geeraerts’s taxonomy of lexicological salience, I propose a multimodal representational framework that distinguishes referential, conceptual, phonological, orthographic, and gestural dimensions of ideophonic lexical items. The framework is used to reinterpret a broad range of previous studies as investigating different manifestations of salience, including highlighting, prototypicality, distributional preference, distinctiveness, sociolinguistic prevalence, entrenchment, and cue matching. The resulting taxonomy integrates corpus-based, experimental, typological, and multimodal approaches while demonstrating that ideophone semantics is increasingly characterized by an emerging onomasiological perspective.

articles.title: The measurement of depression across cognitive abilities in the context of old age: Testing for measurement invariance using local structural equation modeling
articles.authors: Stanisław Konrad Czerwiński; Paweł Andrzej Atroszko; Roman Konarski
articles.abstract: Recent work revealed that measures of mental health might lack measurement invariance across the levels of cognitive abilities. This finding raises concerns for studies on both cognition and mental health, as measurement invariance is a fundamental requirement for meaningful comparisons of variables across a given characteristic. This study aimed to test the measurement invariance of the Center for Epidemiological Studies – Depression (CES-D) scale across five cognitive abilities: crystallized knowledge, quantitative reasoning, verbal fluency, episodic memory, and verbal reasoning. Data from four waves of the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) were used. The samples analyzed consisted of approximately 20,000 participants aged 50 years or older. The results showed that CES-D lacks measurement invariance across all five cognitive abilities measured. A prominent pattern emerged, with unstandardized item thresholds increasing with cognitive abilities. This finding carries major consequences not only for scientific research but also screening for depression and clinical diagnosis.

articles.title: AI Subjectification: Conceptualization and a Layered Framework
articles.authors: Xingyi LIU; Xianglong ZENG
articles.abstract: Recent advances in conversational AI increasingly challenge the traditional instrumental framing, where users in interaction not only utilize AI to accomplish tasks but also begin to place it in a subject position. However, existing theoretical constructs primarily focus on the psychological attributes users ascribe to AI, rather than the normative practices of how AI is concretely treated in relationships. To bridge this conceptual gap, this article proposes the concept of AI Subjectification, defining it as the process by which interactants place AI in a subject position and, on that basis, extend specific treating rules and status expectations to it. Drawing on objectification theory and recent findings in human–computer interaction, we conceptualize AI subjectification as an observable and multidimensional mode of treating in interaction, and construct a Layered Framework of AI subjectification. This framework organizes AI subjectification into the Value Layer (End-regarding orientation), the Relational Interaction Layer (Treat as Autonomous, Treat as Agentic, Treat as Experiencing, Treat as Unique, and Treat as Dignified), and the Institutional Layer (Independence Conferral and Power Conferral), which leads to a series of testable propositions. This article further clarifies the boundaries between AI subjectification and adjacent concepts (anthropomorphism, mind perception, and the Computers as Social Actors paradigm). AI subjectification provides a novel and operationalizable vocabulary for the fields of psychology and human–computer interaction, and offers important implications for the design of AI ethical guidelines, user governance, and the management of human–AI responsibility chains.

articles.title: The ABC of Heuristics: Approximate Bayesian Computation as a Framework for Heuristic Inference
articles.authors: Tianwei Gong; Simon Valentin; Neil R Bramley; Christopher G. Lucas
articles.abstract: Heuristics have long been viewed as simple decision rules that sacrifice optimality for cognitive efficiency. However, this perspective fails to fully account for their effectiveness in complex, real-world environments. This paper proposes a reinterpretation of heuristics as realizations of likelihood-free approximation to Bayesian inference (LFI), bridging the gap between heuristic and normative approaches to decision-making. We argue that many heuristics can be understood as implementations of Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC), where observed data are compared to prior predictions via summary statistics (a form of LFI). This view situates heuristics within a probabilistic framework, explaining how they can represent uncertainty and adapt to environmental structure. Our approach addresses three key challenges in the field: It relaxes strong assumptions about cue-target relationships in heuristic models, accounts for implicit uncertainty representation in heuristic decision-making, and invites a more appropriate benchmark for evaluating heuristics' performance. To demonstrate the practical applicability of our framework, we present two case studies --- a classic cue-based decision task and an ecological causal learning task. These show that an ABC model using summary statistics can well approximate the benchmark performance provided by unconstrained Bayesian inference, explain the apparent emergence of different heuristics given environmental changes, and capture human behaviors better than a rational Bayesian benchmark without introducing new mysteries. By unifying heuristics and Bayesian inference through the lens of likelihood-free methods, this work provides a more nuanced understanding of human decision-making, and provides a bridge to the literature on inference-by-sampling.

articles.title: Cross-Lagged Panel Models for Studying Psychopathology: A Comparative Overview of Structural Equation and Panel Network Approaches
articles.authors: René Freichel; Ilya Milos Veer; Reinout Wiers; Richard J. McNally; Sacha Epskamp
articles.abstract: Researchers have increasingly adopted complex methodological approaches to investigate the co-development of symptoms over longer time frames, such as months and years. Panel studies assess a large group of individuals at multiple time points over an extended period. Various analytical approaches exist for examining the co-development of variables in panel data, yet a comprehensive overview is lacking. This study provides a detailed review and application of four key analytical approaches for examining cross-lagged associations in panel data. The four approaches include two Structural Equation Models (SEM): the Cross- Lagged Panel Model (CLPM) and the Random-Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI- CLPM), along with two network model adaptations: Cross-Lagged Panel Network analysis (CLPN) and Panel Graphical Vector Autoregression Model (GVAR). We describe each method’s distinct characteristics, advantages, and limitations. To illustrate these, we applied these models to a panel dataset of adolescents and young adults (NSPN 2400 cohort study), examining the relationships between impulsivity and symptoms of depression and anxiety. Results showed varying temporal associations, highlighting the importance of model selection based on research objectives and data characteristics. A simulation study demonstrated that models separating within- and between-person effects (panel GVAR, RI- CLPM) reproduced true within-person temporal effects more accurately. Our review highlights the value of using multiple approaches in multiverse analyses to assess the sensitivity of findings to different analytical methods. Ultimately, the choice of analytical method greatly influences how dynamic cross-lagged processes in developmental psychopathology are interpreted, affecting the development and refinement of relevant clinical theories.

articles.title: Large Language Model–Generated Tutoring Responses Receive Higher Ratings but Are Penalized by Source-Based Evaluation Bias
articles.authors: Ola Ozernov-Palchik; Fabio Catania; John Gabrieli; Satrajit S Ghosh
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly positioned as scalable providers of individualized tutoring, yet their pedagogical quality and social reception in authentic K–12 instructional contexts remain understudied. We conducted a factorial experiment in which independent participant samples evaluated identical tutoring responses under different source framing conditions. Adults and K–12 educators evaluated tutoring responses drawn from a randomized controlled trial with third- and fourth-grade students. Human-authored responses were produced by trained tutors during real instructional sessions; matched responses were generated by an LLM from the same conversational contexts. Responses varied in true authorship (human vs. LLM), and separate participant groups evaluated identical response sets told that responses were generated either by humans or by AI. When authorship was held constant, LLM-generated responses were rated as more effective, engaging, and responsive than those written by human tutors. However, identical responses received lower evaluations when attributed to AI, revealing a robust source-based evaluation bias. Computational linguistic analyses showed that AI and human responses were semantically similar but stylistically distinguishable, and that features most strongly associated with higher ratings were largely independent of those differentiating sources. These findings provide an ecologically grounded account of how LLM-generated instructional content is evaluated: LLM responses can match or exceed human responses on perceived pedagogical dimensions while being systematically penalized when attributed to AI.

articles.title: Different Characteristics, Similar Networks: A network analysis of problematic cannabis use among people who use cannabis medicinally or recreationally
articles.authors: Nora de Bode; Nikolaus von Schenck; Emese Kroon; Janna Cousijn
articles.abstract:
Introduction: Currently, most evidence on the impact of regular cannabis use on the risk of problematic use patterns stems from individuals with recreational use motives, while individuals using medicinally may differ in important ways, including use characteristics and experienced problems. Hence, this study directly compared individuals using medicinally or recreationally motives on user characteristics and (networks of) indicators of problematic use, measured using the CUDIT-R. 
Methods: We included 932 individuals aged 18–65 years who used cannabis at least 2–4 times per month. Measures assessed cannabis use characteristics, mental health, and cannabis use severity and related problems. CUDIT-R networks were estimated using a regularized partial correlation (EBICglasso) approach for the full sample and separately by motive (medicinal n = 279, recreational n = 653). Group differences were evaluated using Mann-Whitney U tests (e.g., user characteristics, CUDIT-R scores, mental health) and network comparison tests. 
Results: The medicinal group was on average older, included more women, and reported more comorbidities than the recreational group. Furthermore, the medicinal group used cannabis more frequently, but the recreational group had higher total CUDIT-R scores, indicative of higher use-related problems. The overall CUDIT-R network was dense, with inability to stop and cognitive problems emerging as the most central nodes. Network structure did not differ by motive, although the medicinal group scored lower on most individual CUDIT-R items. 
Conclusions: The CUDIT-R items appear to interact similarly regardless of motive. However, distinct user characteristics and lower item endorsement among those using medicinally indicate that problematic cannabis use may develop differently depending on motive.

articles.title: The access and use of GLP-1 receptor agonists in people with eating disorders in the UK: A mixed method study
articles.authors: Abigail Pickard; Michelle Carroll; Lauren Bruha; Sukriye Acar; Emy Nimbley; Amelia Austin; Helen Sharpe; Fiona Duffy
articles.abstract:
Objective: To explore the use, access, and motivations of individuals with eating disorders (EDs) attempting to access Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) for weight management in the UK.
Method: A mixed-methods convergent parallel design was used. Eligible participants were aged 16+, had an ED, and had attempted to access GLP-1 RAs in the past two years. Seventy-two participants completed an online survey, with quantitative data analysed descriptively and qualitative data analysed thematically. 
Results:  Ninety three percent (n=67) reported current or previous GLP-1 RA’s use and most common motivations were weight loss and binge eating reduction. The most frequent prescriber was online pharmacies (n=52, 74.3%). When prescribed, two thirds were asked about an ED but did not disclose this, one quarter were not asked about EDs. Thirty seven percent (n=25) of participants who received medication did not meet BMI prescription requirements and the approximately half did not receive ongoing monitoring. Qualitative themes found that motivations for using GLP-1 RAs were guided by ED cognitions and recovery, and uncertainty emerged surrounding intentions of long-term use.
Conclusion: Despite screening of ED’s and BMI being recommended, most participants in this study obtained GLP-1 RAs for weight loss with little ongoing monitoring, suggesting the need for more robust regulation.

articles.title: Associations of lifestyle factors and genetic risk with risk and rate advancement periods of dementia
articles.authors: Yating You; Frederick K. Ho; Donald M Lyall; Claire Hastie
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION
Little is understood about the extent to which lifestyle factors can advance or delay the risk of developing dementia, and whether that is dependent on non-modifiable factors, e.g. sex and genetic susceptibility.
METHODS
Among 224,516 UK Biobank participants aged ≥50 years at baseline, Cox regression examined the relations of apolipoprotein E gene (APOE) genotypes, and lifestyle with incident dementia. Rate advancement periods were used to quantify the association between these factors and advancing or delaying incidence rate relative to age.
RESULTS
Over median follow-up of 13.6 years, versus neutral APOE ε3ε3, ε4 presence advanced dementia risk by 5.58 years whereas ε2 presence delayed by 1.08 year (q<0.001). Overall unfavourable lifestyle advanced dementia risk by 1.90 years - specifically, smoking, heavy drinking, and prolonged sedentariness, by 0.64 to 1.52 years (q<0.001). Interactions showed that overall unfavourable lifestyle advanced more dementia risk more among ε2 carriers than ε4 carriers, and ε4 presence advanced more in females than males.
DISCUSSION
Overall unfavourable lifestyle and APOE ε4 genotype advanced dementia risk independently by almost 2 and 6 years respectively, with significant gene-lifestyle and gene-sex interactions. Lifestyle’s benefit on cognitive preservation is to some extent sex and genotype-specific, which targeted intervention does not currently consider.

articles.title: Overprotective parenting and Socio-economic stressors: Mapping the Connections Using a Network Approach
articles.authors: Maria Bacikova-Sleskova; Gabriel Baník; Lucia Barbierik; Stijn Van Petegem
articles.abstract:
Despite overprotective parenting being a major concern for optimal adolescent development, it is highly prevalent among contemporary parents. This study uses network analyses to explore how socio-economic status (SES) and various socio-economic stressors are related to overprotective parenting, including academic overinvolvement. Moreover, it explores the moderating role of family income as a measure of objective SES. Parents of adolescents (N = 697, Mage = 46.4, SD = 5.17; 84.3% mothers) completed measures of overprotective parenting, academic overinvolvement, family income, subjective socio-economic status, financial scarcity, perceived competitiveness, income inequality perceptions, job insecurity and threat perceptions.
The network analysis revealed a stable structure in which helicoptering and infantilization emerged as the most central components of overprotective parenting. Although most associations were positive, assignment tracking was negatively associated with privacy violation while dependency messaging was negatively associated with overprotectiveness. Socio-economic stressors formed a closely interconnected cluster but showed generally weak associations with overprotective parenting. The strongest links involved subjective SES which was negatively associated with overprotectiveness and academic overinvolvement as well as threat perceptions, particularly danger perception. The bridge analyses identified financial scarcity, worry as threat perception, danger perception and academic overinvolvement as potential links between socio-economic stressors and overprotective parenting. The moderation analyses showed no moderation effect of family income on the associations. Overall, the study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of overprotective parenting that can be influenced by broader social and economic pressures.

articles.title: Factors Associated With Weight Loss Success: An Umbrella Review and the DELTA Grid Taxonomy
articles.authors: Kari Kuulman; Kadri Arumäe; Senta Karus; Uku Vainik
articles.abstract: Identifying who succeeds at weight loss, and why, is a long-standing problem in psychological and behavioural science. Numerous predictors have been identified, but evidence is scattered across reviews focused on narrow domains, where inconsistent terminology raises construct-validity (jingle-jangle) concerns and existing taxonomies rely on a single dimension. The field thus lacks an integrated, cross-domain map of which factors are associated with weight outcomes, where they reside, and how they operate. This umbrella review aimed to build a broad, cross-domain inventory of factors and a classification framework. We searched five databases for reviews published between 2014 and 2024, supplemented by citation tracking. Forty-nine reviews spanning 1,118 unique primary studies (138,153 participants across the 27 reviews reporting aggregate totals) yielded 992 unique original factor descriptions, consolidated into 96 evidence-based factors using established psychological frameworks rather than ad hoc grouping. The DELTA Grid classifies each factor by its ecological location (biological, psychological, habitual, relational, or environmental) and the mechanism through which it operates (affective, behavioural, cognitive, or desire/motivational). Behavioural mechanisms dominated (50.0%), while affective mechanisms (11.5%) and the relational-network domain (3.1%) were scarce; 6 of 20 cells (30%) were empty. These imbalances likely reflect research traditions and the current evidence base. The DELTA Grid reveals structural patterns and blind spots that unidimensional approaches obscure, and offers a basis for future multidimensional assessment and intervention.

articles.title: Effects of a Theory-Based Smartphone Intervention to Decrease Neuroticism in the General Public
articles.authors: Amanda Jo Wright; Peter Haehner; Rosalie Andrae; Till Lubczyk; Christopher James Hopwood; Wiebke Bleidorn
articles.abstract: Many people wish to be less neurotic and such decreases could have far-reaching benefits, but evidence on nonclinical interventions and change mechanisms is limited. Using a German-speaking sample (N = 446), we conducted a 6-week, smartphone-based randomized controlled intervention to test effects of theory-based strategies targeting different neuroticism levels and aspects. Across groups, there were significant self-report effects (d[effect] = -0.22 to -0.37) that persisted through a 2-month follow-up (d[effect] = -0.16 to -0.33) and follow-up peer-report effects for one of two measures (d[effect] = -0.18 to -0.30). Treatment group comparisons indicated that state-level strategies fostered larger immediate albeit shorter-lasting effects, whereas habit-level strategies led to smaller initial declines that strengthened over time. Behavior-focused strategies, for states and especially habits, yielded particularly strong effects across assessment methods, both independently and incrementally. Our findings demonstrate that neuroticism can be changed within 6 weeks and provide insight into effective mechanisms of change.

articles.title: Retrieval Stopping in Delayed Fear Extinction
articles.authors: Maike Bersch; Stephanie M. Ashton; Martyna Emanuela Gwiazda; Conny W.E.M. Quaedflieg
articles.abstract: Intrusive thoughts following traumatic experiences are common and may be conditioned responses to trauma cues. Fear extinction reduces these responses. The timing of extinction influences its underlying mechanisms, with delayed extinction facilitating inhibitory learning. Recent models suggest that active retrieval stopping contributes to extinction via inhibitory control mechanisms. Using a modified Extinction-Think/No-Think paradigm to target the inhibitory retrieval mechanism of extinction, this study examines whether retrieval stopping enhances delayed fear extinction. Fifty-nine healthy participants learned aversive object-scene pairs followed by a fear acquisition phase. After 24 hours, participants underwent extinction whilst practising retrieval stopping. We hypothesised greater reductions in unconditioned stimulus (US) expectancy for objects following retrieval stopping (No-Think) than standard extinction (View) over time. The results showed that US expectancy decreased during extinction, though retrieval stopping was not superior to standard extinction.  Bayesian analysis provided weak evidence that intentional retrieval stopping is not a superior alternative to standard extinction. Further research should investigate the long-term effects of retrieval stopping on fear recovery and generalisation.

articles.title: Longitudinal Attendance Trajectories Across Three Academic Years in English Secondary Schools: Predictors and links with Internalising Symptoms
articles.authors: Christopher Knowles; Qiqi Cheng; Emma Thornton; Neil Humphrey
articles.abstract: Objective:  To identify longitudinal attendance trajectories across secondary education, examine their eco-systemic predictors, and assess associations with emotional difficulties.  Method: Linked #BeeWell survey and administrative data were analysed for 28,736 pupils aged 12–13 at baseline across 156 secondary schools in Greater Manchester. Piecewise latent growth mixture modelling identified attendance trajectories across nine consecutive school terms (Autumn, Spring and Summer terms 2021/22–2023/24). Multinomial logistic regression examined predictors across individual, family, school, peer, and community domains. Emotional difficulties were modelled as a latent growth process to compare class-specific intercepts and slopes.  Results: Three attendance trajectories were identified: Consistently High (92.4%), Progressive Decline (5.1%), and Decline & Recover (2.5%). Socioeconomic disadvantage was most strongly associated with sub-optimal attendance trajectories (ORs = 2.94–4.97), with dose–response effects for neighbourhood deprivation. Special educational needs were also associated with increased risk, while protective factors included good physical health, sufficient sleep, school belonging, and minoritised ethnic group membership. LGBTQ+ identity was not independently associated in fully adjusted models. Pupils following sub-optimal trajectories reported higher emotional difficulties at baseline (d ≈ .34–.41), but no differences in rates of change over time were observed.  Conclusion: Attendance trajectories are socially patterned and linked to pre-existing vulnerabilities. Emotional difficulties appear to precede, rather than result from, divergence in attendance. Findings support multi-tiered interventions combining universal strategies to promote school belonging with targeted support addressing socioeconomic disadvantage and mental health needs. Evidence of a recovery trajectory highlights the potential for timely intervention during secondary education.

articles.title: Feeling academia: An in-depth analysis of researchers’ achievement emotions
articles.authors: Lara Abel; Luisa Ciampi; Mollie Etheridge; Allison Beggs; Yingjie Li; Molly Smih; Noam Tal-Perry; ARRC - Debbie Birkett; Marie Collier; Katherine M. Dawson
articles.abstract: This study uses a combination of qualitative research methods for an in-depth examination of Early Career Researchers’ (ECRs) and Principal Investigators’ (PIs) achievement emotions and emotion management strategies at a research-intensive UK university. As part of an online survey, 15 ECRs and eight PIs submitted reflective letters providing rich insights into their professional lives. We interviewed five participants to deepen our understanding of their experiences. Our qualitative analysis combined thematic and affective coding, drawing on appraisal theories of emotion. We found that positive emotions were reported in relation to aspects inherent to the academic professions, both in relation to teaching and research, including supporting others and fulfilment in research. Negative emotions related to structural conditions including precarity, low pay and lack of institutional support. Participants highlighted the importance of social and personal resources for coping with the negative emotions associated with these structural issues. Through the process of letter writing, participants actively regulated their emotions using reappraisal and self-reassurance mechanisms. We discuss how narrative research methods, such as the letter methodology, can be used as powerful action research tools for studying and intervening on academic emotions and propose workshop formats as levers for improving academics’ professional experiences.
